#9130. Christie’s Notches a $145.9 M. Sale of 21st-Century Art, Led by a $32.9 M. Basquiat, amid Flagging Energy

By Brian Boucher, Harrison Jacobs November 19, 2026 10:49pm

Christie’s finished out New York’s fall auction week on Thursday evening at its Rockefeller Center salesroom, bringing in $145.9 million in a 56-lot sale of 21st-century art (after works by Jeff Koons and Ed Ruscha, estimated to sell for as much as $11 million between them, were withdrawn). Leading the sale was a $32.9 million Jean-Michel Basquiat painting that fell just shy of its low estimate.

The sale included 20 works from the collection of Antonio Homem, longtime director of the storied Sonnabend Gallery, which was founded by his adoptive mother, Ileana Sonnabend. Sold to benefit their foundation, the works totaled $41.9 million. Also on offer were 10 works from the estate of beloved New York philanthropist Agnes Gund, who died last year, totaling $25.7 million. Related Articles Piaget's Latest Release Is a Limited-Edition Andy Warhol Camouflage Watch A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie's Day Sale

After the withdrawals, the sale was estimated to bring between $126 million and $192 million; the hammer total on the night fell considerably shy at $117.7 million. Over the two-hour sale, the house found buyers for 51 lots, for a sell-through rate of 91 percent. Works by John Currin, William Eggleston, Wade Guyton, Gerhard Richter, and Yayoi Kusama failed to sell.

Many prominent advisors were in the room, including Erica Barrish, Amy Cappellazzo, Ralph DeLuca, and Gabriela Palmieri, as well as well-known dealers like Marianne Boesky, Jeanne Greenberg Rohatyn, and Christophe Van de Weghe. But there were a notable number of empty seats, and the atmosphere was unmistakably enervated after a long week of sales.

The sale started inauspiciously, with the first 19 lots, all from the Sonnabend collection, failing to hammer above their estimates. Bidding picked up only on the final lot of that trove, Jean Prouvé’s Table “Centrale” (“Trapèze”), petit modèle. The piece sold after five minutes of bidding between several specialists and a bidder in the room, before Sara Friedlander, Christie’s chairman of postwar and contemporary art in the Americas, nabbed it with a winning bid of $1.3 million. With fees, the total came to $1.7 million on a $700,000–$1 million estimate. But, all told, 10 of the 20 Sonnabend lots hammered below estimate. The collection hammered for $33.4 million, or $41.9 million with fees, against a pre-sale estimate of $35.25 million to $53.15 million (minus the withdrawn Koons, Wild Boy and Puppy). Not great any way you slice it.

The most notable of the Sonnabend works was Andy Warhol’s 1962 painting Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), tagged at $6–$8 million. The soup cans show one of Warhol’s most iconic images and are practically synonymous with Pop art. Adrien Meyer, global head of private sales and the auctioneer at Tuesday evening’s 20th-century sale, traded bids with a bidder in the room, who nailed it down with a $7.3 million bid, translating to $9 million all in.

Also from the trove was Roy Lichtenstein’s Large Spool (1963). Standing nearly six feet high, the work had been off the market since the Sonnabends bought it from Leo Castelli Gallery four years after it was painted. It has hung in museums all over the world, and its sale comes amid a major Lichtenstein retrospective at New York’s Whitney Museum of American Art. Auctioneer Yu-Ge Wang tossed out a handful of absentee bids from the rostrum before Friedlander got it for her client with a $7 million bid, for a total of $8.6 million with fees. The work’s pre-sale estimate was $10 million to $15 million.

Jeff Koons’s six-foot-high sculpture Hulk (Friends), 2004–12, also from the Sonnabend collection, shows the comic-book hero with small creatures perched on his shoulders and was estimated at $3.5–$5.5 million. It hammered after only a few bids at $3.3 million, or $4.15 million with fees, to the house’s Michael Baptist. (Koons was also a seller this week, bringing seven artworks to auction at Christie’s on Tuesday night, totaling $104 million.)

Bidding improved marginally from there, but for the most part, this was a sleepy sale. Even the biggest attraction of the night, Basquiat’s much-touted painting Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), which dates to 1983 and measures seven feet square, failed to generate much excitement. Wang opened the bidding at $23 million, and for a few long moments it seemed there would be no bids. Then Ana Maria Celis, head of postwar and contemporary art, rescued the painting, beating out Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president and global chairman of 20th- and 21st-century art. It hammered at $28 million and sold for $32.9 million with the house’s fees.

The hammer price was just shy of the $30–$50 million estimate. But the work, inspired by a sketch by Leonardo da Vinci, had been off the market for two decades, so the seller no doubt made a tidy profit. The painter’s auction market has famously exploded in the intervening years: every one of his paintings to sell for more than $10 million, all 83 of them, has done so since then.

The large canvas, featuring the artist’s trademark scratchy messages and the titular sketchy heads against an orange background, had appreciated enormously since its previous trips to the block. It appeared at Sotheby’s London in 2000, when it fetched just above $400,000, within estimate, and again at the same house five years later, when it tripled in value to bring an above-estimate $1.3 million.

Vija Celmins’s 1990 painting Untitled (Ocean) was one of the few lots of the evening to generate a genuine bidding war. The painting came from the Gund estate; Gund bought it the year after it was painted. It drew bids from Joanna Szymkowiak, head of private sales; Arco Yu, a Christie’s Hong Kong specialist; and a woman bidding in the room. For four minutes, the three traded incremental bids until the room bidder won out. Still, that brought the hammer to only $5.75 million, just under the $6 million low estimate. With fees, the total came to $7.1 million.

The 10 Gund works fared better than those from the Sonnabend collection, hammering for $20.4 million on a $16.95 million to $24.65 million pre-sale estimate. With fees, the total squeaked past the high estimate to reach $25.7 million.

There wasn’t much rhythm to the proceedings. A 1990 Gerhard Richter Abstraktes Bild painting from the estate of legendary art dealer Marian Goodman, who long represented the artist and bought the work from him that year, carried a $6 million to $8 million estimate. It failed to sell after garnering no bids. Three lots later, another Abstraktes Bild, from 1991, measuring three feet square and dominated by red, blue, and green, sparked a short contest between Friedlander and Rotter. Rotter eventually won it with a $7.6 million bid. With fees, the total came to $9.4 million. The painting’s pre-sale estimate was $7 million to $10 million.

“The estimates were too high for this market,” Greenberg Rohatyn told ARTnews on her way out of the salesroom partway through the night. “We need to readjust, and the houses need to be at the forefront of managing expectations.”

Boesky agreed that the estimates were too high. “And the energy was low,” she said on her way out. “The lots that were estimated too high were punished, and those estimated low were rewarded.”

On a brighter note, a few records were notched: Jim Nutt ($1.1 million), Antonio Santín ($486,400), and Julia Jo ($409,600).

The Jo, a swirling, gestural abstraction of fiery oranges and yellows breaking against cool blues and teals, was the night’s final lot, estimated at $30,000–$50,000. Sold to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, the abstraction generated arguably the most spirited bidding of the evening. Wang opened bidding at $20,000, and it quickly climbed into the hundreds of thousands as a cacophony of specialists and a bidder in the room called out bids. It eventually went to the room bidder at a hammer price of $320,000, or $403,200 with fees. That set off a hearty round of applause, at least for one lot.

The sale finished out an auction week that started Monday with a two-part $378.7 million Sotheby’s auction including works from cable television magnate Ted Baum and interior designer Ruth Baum as well as a various-owner The Now and Contemporary sale. Christie’s staged a nearly three-hour 20th-century sale on Tuesday that totaled $626.6 million, led by a record-breaking $85.8 million abstraction by Wassily Kandinsky, closely followed by an $82.3 million landscape by Gustav Klimt. The same night, Phillips sold $104.4 million in modern and contemporary art on Tuesday, led by a $44.6 million Amedeo Modigliani sculpture. On Wednesday, Sotheby’s staged a $777.8 million Impressionist and modern art sale, led by a record-breaking $190.4 million Vincent van Gogh.

#9129. Was Grandma Moses a Foil to Modernity, or a Product of It?

Grandma Moses’s landmark survey at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Arkansas opens with a flash of fire. A scene of a bridge burning in Troy is ablaze in red and orange; another painting, Fire in the Woods (1940), crackles with flames and smoke. This emphasis on fire, thunderstorms, and extreme weather in the first room seems to be an anticipatory rebuke to any potential complaints about Moses’s relentless good cheer. Despite a long and often sorrow-filled life—Anna Mary Robertson (“Grandma”) Moses lost five of her 10 children in infancy—Moses held fast to life’s joys in her art, and most of the paintings in the show are happy scenes of work, celebration, and family. Related Articles Sharif Bey Wins Inaugural Spector Craft Prize At The Momentary, Lucy Sparrow Transforms a Supermarket into a Felt Wonderland

Starting with fire does prime the viewer to recognize the heat of Moses’s oeuvre, an intensity she channeled into careful, repetitive marks—tidy stacks of hay, carefully shaded leaves, the checkered grid of farm fields. Cambridge Valley (1942) is a scene of steady eye, mind, and hand, an expansive view of the New York countryside rendered with lovingly topographic attention. There’s almost no loss of detail as you look across the valley, a result of Moses’s unhurried care. People appear in nearly all her works, simply rendered and adding elements of humor, like a man’s hat blown off by the wind in 1948’s The Thunderstorm, a perfect “O” flush against the picture plane. The fire returns, however, in Moses’s many maple sugaring scenes, flames licking the base of large pots in which sap is boiled down. Even snow scenes are made to sparkle, radiating light through Moses’s use of glitter, a new technology she applied amply to her canvases against the advice of her dealer.

Moses was no stranger to patient work, having spent her life on farms in New York state and Virginia’s Shenandoah Valley. Her memory of these years provided ample subject matter for the painting she took up in her late 70s, though one of the claims of the exhibition was that Moses was making art her whole life. A fireboard from 1918 was what she called her first “large picture,” while yarn pictures from the 1930s show her capacity to work with a limited palette of solid colors. These craft activities, usually cordoned off from the realm of serious art, gave Moses a point of entry into visual representation as a way of telling her own story.

Spanning 101 years, from 1860 to 1961, her life story ran parallel with a century of massive transformation and the rapid emergence of a modern, industrial world. That her style and subject matter remain largely unchanged over the course of her decades-long painting career—the 80 some works in the show have more similarities than differences—suggests Moses’s indifference to the revolutions happening around her. Instead, the exhibition catalog argues, Moses was in dialog with changing notions of the elderly, the increasing representation of labor in 20th-century art, and Cold War politics that sought to export a vision of American goodness.

Was Grandma Moses a foil to modernity, or a product of it? While her work eschews direct portrayals of industry, she reportedly solved the compositional dilemma of capturing sprawling valleys by glimpsing a reflection in a hubcap, introducing the gleam of the automobile into what feel like entirely timeless views. Her art was held up by contemporaries as an example of the “primitive,” exhibited as the quaint musings of an aging farmwife. She seemed to give America a soul, something it appeared to be lacking in the postwar era of big capital. And yet she amassed quite a lot of capital herself, through lucrative partnerships with Hallmark among other companies. She was media-savvy, appearing on talk shows and in documentaries, leveraging the perceived powerlessness of a little old woman to charm and disarm her critics. In the end, there’s nothing more modern than nostalgia for the lost authenticity of the countryside, an authenticity Moses returns us to in her sincerely merry paintings.

#9128. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

SLEEPY SALE. Christie’s topped the tail end of a week of auctions on Thursday evening in New York, bringing in $145.9 million worth of 21st-century art, reports ARTnews. But with the hammer total of $117.7 million, the two-hour sale fell considerably short of its estimate (including withdrawals), which had been set for between $126 million and $192 million. SOFT LANDING. The Landing, a beloved Los Angeles gallery whose program was built around imaginative pairings of historical and contemporary artists, announced it had closed, reports ARTnews. “It has been a privilege to champion extraordinary artists, present ambitious exhibitions, and create a space for meaningful exchange and discovery,” wrote gallery founder and owner Gerard O’Brien on the gallery website. “End of an era,” he added in an Instagram post. O’Brien founded the Landing in 2012 as an offshoot of his design-focused Reform Gallery. “I never really thought there was a big difference,” he said of design and art. The Landing’s roster included four deceased artists (Jeremy Anderson, Richard Bowman, Leslie Kerr, and Fred Reichman) and five living artists (Yevgeniya Baras, Ryan Fenchel, Matt Phillips, Jonathan Ryan, and Amanda Valdez). Several LA galleries have shuttered of late, including Murmurs, the Box, LA Louver, Blum, plus the outposts of Marian Goodman Gallery and Tanya Bonakdar. “While our gallery doors have closed, our commitment to art and artists continues. Watch this space for news of future off-site exhibitions, activations, and special projects,” wrote O’Brien on the gallery website.

An extremely rare abstract, geometric painting by Hilma af Klint from the 1920s sold for $12.7 million at Bukowskis auction house in Stockholm, nearly 16 times its $800,000 high estimate, and a new auction record for the artist. [The Wall Street Journal]

Artist Sarah Sze asks: “How do you make animate and valuable the most throwaway, inanimate material—something that we recognize and then have to understand anew?” in the context of three current projects underway for the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Barclays Center in Brooklyn, and the Yale University Art Gallery in New Haven. [The New York Times]

Mercedes-Benz is auctioning its rare CII supercar, to raise millions to develop its own museum in Stuttgart. [Monopol]

IMMERSED IN WHAT? Is immersive digital art a new phenomenon, or the latest evolution of what artists have been trying to do for centuries? Ocula’s Nathalie Olah explores that question with examples from throughout art history. She goes from the “panorama,” an 18th- and 19th-century leisure activity that included admiring mural-length paintings of various exotic landscapes, to Louis Daguerre’s moving, continuous paintings on translucent fabrics, and his early forms of photography. Read on to decide where the similarities and the stark differences lie between these past and present works, and whether we ultimately truly feel “immersed,” or anything at all.

#9126. Reims 502 uses pink palette for "non-referential" commercial building in Mexico

A stepped facade fronts this pink commercial building in Mexico called Rosadoce, designed by local studio Reims 502 to suit various tenants over its lifespan.

Rosadoce is located in a low-density residential neighbourhood near the historic centre of Querétaro, a state in north-central Mexico, which is redeveloping into a mixed-use area.

The studio said the 840-square-metre building was “conceived as an adaptable urban asset” that can function as a single unit, four independent commercial spaces or sixteen smaller modules, ensuring its longevity and usability well into the future.

“Rosadoce by Reims 502 is a flexible commercial building in Querétaro, Mexico, designed as an adaptable urban platform for work, commerce and public life,” said the studio.

“Designed during the pandemic, it rethinks commercial architecture in response to changing patterns of work, consumption and urban life.”

Local planning constraints determined the building’s scale, while its “non-referential form” evolved from various design strategies, the studio said.

It reaches seven metres in height – the maximum height allowed above street level – which led the studio to carve out a semi-basement level to increase usable area.

Above ground are two open-plan levels, organised around a central stair and punctured by vertical voids that naturally light and ventilate the building.

Meanwhile, the basement currently contains service spaces including parking and plant rooms. However, similarly to the rest of the building, it has an open-plan layout to support future commercial activity.

Crowning Rosadoce is a usable rooftop filled with planters that provide thermal insulation.

“The inverted-stair facade creates horizontal openings for daylight and views while regulating visual permeability from the street,” said the studio.

“Because the building’s future uses remain open-ended, the facade avoids excessive transparency and provides a controlled threshold between public exposure and interior flexibility.”

The pink render that colours the building’s exterior, provided by lime-based products manufacturer Nanocal, was chosen as a nod to the rose-colored quarry stone that defines Querétaro’s historic centre.

This same colour was used throughout the project, with the steel structure, concrete blockwork, grilles and service equipment all finished in the same tone, creating a warm feel for the interior.

According to the studio, the building’s future flexibility is achieved through the combination of open plans as well as “exposed construction, passive environmental strategies and an active rooftop”.

“This allows it to respond to different economic scenarios, tenant profiles, subletting arrangements and future programmes without major structural alterations,” said Reims 502.

The project is on the eight-strong shortlist for the small workplace interior category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards.

Other pink buildings in Mexico include a co-living apartment block with a series of arched forms by Estudio Zero and a minimalist house sandwiched between two buildings by César Béjar Studio.

#9124. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#9123. Hilma af Klint Painting Sells in Sweden for $12.7 M., Setting New Auction Record

A Hilma af Klint painting sold at a Swedish auction house on Thursday for $12.7 million with fees, setting a record for the artist, whose work does not often make it to the market. That sum is about 15 times the work’s high estimate of $800,000.

The painting, a 1920 abstraction called Ser III No. 5, made it to auction in a sale of modern art and design at Bukowskis in Stockholm. Prior to the auction, it had been held since 1995 by the same unnamed family, who had obtained it after af Klint’s foundation deaccessioned what Bukowski described as “a small number of works.” Related Articles In Rare Market Moment, Hilma af Klint Painting Comes to Auction in Sweden A Stunning Survey of Spirits and Séances Takes Over a Baroque Palace

Its sale is merely the latest chapter in af Klint’s posthumous ascent. The artist, who died in 1944, was little-known until a series of well-attended museum exhibitions in the 2010s repositioned her as a pioneering figure in the history of European modernism.

A Guggenheim Museum exhibition in 2018—one that shattered attendance records at the New York institution—positioned her as the inventor of abstraction. She made her paintings in response to spirits she contacted; what resulted were dazzling arrays of curlicuing lines, enigmatic shapes, and Inscrutable symbols.

Her foundation has generally kept her work off the market, as some of her descendants argue that she did not produce her art for commercial consumption. Yet the foundation’s position on her art and legacy has been controversial in some corners, leading certain art historians to question whether her descendants have misunderstood af Klint’s intentions.

At least one art historian argued this week that the Bukowskis sale was wrong. Rachel Villari, who wrote her dissertation on af Klint, told NPR, “For me, I don’t believe that you can put a price on her work. And I believe that that makes it even more desirable to people who can afford to buy her work because what would you want more than the impossible painting that you’re not supposed to have or can’t have, right? And if it’s sold, the public won’t be able to ever see that painting or have access to it again.” (As is common with auction sales, Bukowskis did not name the buyer of the af Klint.)

Bukowskis treated the sale as a victory, with CEO Louise Arén saying in a statement, “It is remarkable in itself to sell an abstract work by Hilma af Klint. The exceptional final price marks a historic moment, and all of us at Bukowskis are incredibly happy and proud.”

#9122. Tant A Temps Design "restores the visual characteristics of Tang architecture" in Chinese cafe

Local practice Tant A Temps Design aimed to revive the aesthetics of the Tang Dynasty when designing the interiors for cafe Laibei 1087, located in a historical building in Xi’an, China.

The cafe sits inside the Beilin Museum, originally constructed in 1087 to preserve stone steles inscribed with Confucian philosophy and famous calligraphic works.

The timber columns and beams of the historic building were preserved, with the same approach extended into the cafe interiors.

Guided by a “minimum intervention” and “zero damage” renovation strategy, Tant A Temps Design made every new addition detachable and reversible, which allowed the building’s original features to remain untouched.

In the cafe, the furniture is suspended from wooden beams or arranged around columns to avoid direct contact with the original structures.

Tant A Temps Design also created tables, chairs and display cabinets with designs that draw from elements of the ancient building framework, such as the beams, columns and dougong brackets.

Lightweight and prefabricated materials and modular systems were used throughout the space.

For the main colour palette, Tant A Temps Design chose light green hues complemented by gold accents.

“The purpose of choosing this colour scheme is to restore the visual characteristics of Tang architecture – robust, imposing and richly coloured,” the studio explained.

“Abandoning the rigid replication of ancient architecture, it extracts and reshapes the spiritual core of Tang and Song aesthetics through a restrained colour palette and minimalist structural language, creating a serene and elegant atmosphere that highly matches the cultural temperament of the Stele Forest.”

An integrated functional island was designed to function as the central bar counter.

All modern utility systems, including air conditioning, water, electricity, lighting and exhausts, were concealed and integrated into the top and bottom of the bar counter.

This is consistent with the studio’s commitment to preserving the heritage building while giving it a contemporary, functional upgrade.

“This forms a functional system that is both independent of the original building structure and seamlessly integrated into the historical environment, setting a new paradigm for the adaptive reuse of similar cultural heritage buildings,” said the studio.

The cafe is part of a 220-square-metre development that also includes a rest area, a retail zone and a stone-rubbing workshop that serves as a history learning centre.

According to Tant A Temps Design, the project has transformed a dormant historical building into an accessible and interactive cultural space.

Led by founder Wei Chen, Tant A Temps Design is an interior design practice based in Xi’an.

Elsewhere in China, Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou and Keiji Ashizawa designed an “open and inviting retail space” in the historic building in Shanghai.

#9121. MoMA PS1 Plans ‘Malvestir,’ Exhibition Looking at Latin American and Latinx Fashion and Contemporary Art

MoMA PS1 in New York will open a major exhibition next spring looking at the connections between the spheres of Latin American and Latinx fashion and contemporary art.

Opening April 22, “Malvestir” will feature the work of 20 artists and designers, including Willy Chavarria, Camila Falquez, Carla Fernández, Bárbara Sánchez-Kane, Troy Montes Michie, Manauara Clandestina, and La Cholla Jackson, among others. It will be curated by PS1 director Connie Butler and associate curator Elena Ketelsen González. Related Articles ARTnews Awards 2026 Established Artist of the Year: Vaginal Davis Have Fashion Folk Ruined the Frieze London Experience?

The exhibition’s title comes from a portmanteau with a long history that combines the prefix “mal-” (meaning poorly) and the verb “vestir” (to dress). Per a release, the “historical term [was] used in Spanish colonial dress codes that policed caste, race, and gender, labeling those who transgressed social boundaries or refused to comply as malvestidos.” While still a pejorative in contemporary Spanish, the release adds, that the term has been embraced as “a countercultural charge, as a deliberate rejection of Eurocentric taste and class decorum, or queer disobedience.”

Art museums have increasingly embraced fashion exhibitions in recent years, at times pairing garments with contemporary art. PS1’s, however, was ahead of the curve: the institution exhibited fashion between 1980 and 1984 through its Multi-Disciplinary Program. The program was facilitated by the late Hollywood stylist and make-up artist Di Russo, who also served as its curator. Projects staged during the program’s run, including ones by Julio (1980), Homer Layne / Charles James (1981), Willi Smith (1982), and Betsey Johnson (1983), have been partially restaged for the museum’s current exhibition “New York Fashion at PS1, 1980–1984” (through March 15).

Among the pairings that will feature in “Malvestir” are the exaggerated proportions of Chavarria’s designs that draw from Chicanx fashion; the “Dominican-York” streetwear and queer nightlight fashions of LUAR; Falquez’s photographic portraits of queer and trans people; and Clandestina’s mixed-media installation TRANSCLANDESTINA 3020, which was commissioned for the 2025 Bienal de São Paulo.

Other themes that will be explored in the exhibition include the circulation and appropriation of Indigenous craft and aesthetics by Western designers and artists, Eurocentric notions of beauty standards and class aspirations, and the textile waste—called “pacas”—that is imported from the United States throughout Latin America.

“Over the past few years, we visited artists’ studios across the US, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America, and again and again we found artists and designers using the language of fashion to confront the commodification of identity, waste colonialism, and the pull of class aspirationalism,” Ketelsen González told ARTnews in an email. “Malvestir brings together some of the most exciting artists working today to show both the possibilities and the contradictions embedded in the politics of dress.”

The oneworld partnership route to Qatar business class using AA miles

## Flying Qatar QSuites for 70,000 Miles: The Redemption That Feels Impossible Until You Do It Imagine settling into your own private suite — a door that actually closes, a fully flat bed measuring 80 inches long, a 21.5-inch 4K screen, and a meal service that rivals the best business-class restaurants at 40,000 feet. Qatar Airways QSuites isn't just the best business class product in the sky right now; it's the product that frequent flyers describe as the moment they understood why people obsess over travel rewards. And you can book it for 70,000 American AAdvantage miles one-way. Let that sink in. The same seat — Washington Dulles to Doha, with the ability to continue to dozens of destinations across Asia, Africa, and beyond — retails for **$5,000 to $9,000 in cash**. At 70,000 AAdvantage miles, you're extracting between **7.1 and 12.9 cents per point**. The ChooseFI community benchmarks a "good" redemption at 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This redemption is *three to six times that*. This is what the FI community means when we talk about travel rewards as a genuine wealth multiplier. If you've been stockpiling points wondering whether they're actually worth something, this is your answer. A cash ticket that costs more than many people's monthly take-home salary becomes nearly free with the right points strategy. The inefficiency exists because AAdvantage still prices partner awards — flights on airlines like Qatar, JAL, and Cathay Pacific — on a **fixed partner award chart** rather than the dynamic pricing it uses for American-operated flights. Qatar, as a oneworld alliance member, is required to make award space available to partner programs. American prices that space at a flat 70,000 miles for business class, regardless of what Qatar itself charges in cash or its own Avios currency. The result is a structural arbitrage opportunity: you're using a fixed-price chart to book a premium product that Qatar prices at whatever the market will bear — and the market bears a *lot* for QSuites. The ChooseFI community has long understood that the highest-leverage use of points isn't domestic economy upgrades. It's premium international cabin redemptions where the gap between cash price and points cost is widest. On that spectrum, QSuites via AAdvantage sits near the very top.

The core insight here is understanding two separate pricing systems operating simultaneously. Qatar Airways prices its QSuites cabin dynamically in cash — demand surges around holidays, business travel seasons, and major events can push that $5,000 base price to $9,000 or beyond. But American AAdvantage doesn't care about any of that. As a oneworld alliance partner, AAdvantage uses a fixed partner award chart for Qatar redemptions: 70,000 miles one-way in business class, full stop.

This means the more expensive the cash ticket gets, the better your CPP becomes — without you doing anything differently. Book during peak travel periods when cash prices spike to $9,000, and you're extracting 12.9 cents per AAdvantage mile. Even at the floor — a $5,000 cash ticket — you're at 7.1 cents per point. Both numbers are extraordinary.

AAdvantage periodically runs "Web Specials" — discounted partner awards where pricing drops significantly below the standard chart. On Qatar routes, these have historically appeared at 50,000 miles one-way for business class. At 50K miles against a $5,000 cash ticket, your CPP jumps to 10 cents per point. These specials are unpredictable and availability is limited, but if you're flexible on travel dates, checking AA.com regularly for Web Specials on Qatar routes can yield an even better deal.

AAdvantage doesn't have a direct credit card transfer relationship with most major bank currencies the way Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards do. Your primary transfer paths are:

One of the most important nuances of this redemption: AAdvantage has a low fuel surcharge policy. When you book Qatar metal through AAdvantage, you pay government taxes and carrier fees, but AAdvantage does not pass through the fuel surcharges that Qatar would charge if you booked through its own program. This can save hundreds of dollars compared to booking QSuites through Avios or Qatar Privilege Club directly. Always verify fees at checkout, but expect to pay $50–$150 in fees rather than the $500+ you might see through other programs.

Doha isn't just a destination — it's Qatar's hub, and connecting through DOH opens the entire Qatar network. A flight to DOH becomes a connection point for onward travel to destinations across South Asia, Southeast Asia, the Indian Subcontinent, and East Africa, all on the same premium aircraft and the same 70,000-mile award. The IAD→DOH route is one of the best-documented entry points into this system.

You need 70,000 AAdvantage miles in your account before you can book. AAdvantage miles never expire, so there's no urgency pressure once you've accumulated them. If you're short, identify your transfer path:

Do not transfer points until you have confirmed award availability. Points transfers are one-directional and non-reversible.

Go to aa.com and use the "Redeem Miles" search tool. Select:

AAdvantage shows partner award availability directly on its search tool. You're looking for saver-level availability on Qatar-operated flights (flight numbers beginning with QR). These will display at 70,000 miles. If you see higher pricing, that's dynamic partner pricing — keep searching different dates.

Availability on QSuites is the biggest challenge in this redemption. Qatar releases award space to partner programs inconsistently. Search up to 331 days in advance — AAdvantage's full booking window. Earlier searches give you the best selection. Midweek departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) tend to surface more availability than Fridays and Sundays.

Not every Qatar 777-300ER flies QSuites. Before you commit, verify the specific equipment. You can cross-reference on expertflyer.com (paid subscription) or check the seat map within the booking flow — QSuites will show the distinctive 1-2-1 reverse-herringbone configuration with double suites in the center.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific date and flight, initiate your points transfer. Use Citi (instant) or Bilt (1-2 days) if you need speed. After transfer posts, return to AA.com and complete the booking. Have your passport information ready — international bookings require it at checkout.

American Airlines and Qatar Airways are both members of the oneworld alliance, which means AAdvantage miles can book any Qatar-operated award flight at AA's published partner rates. The sweet spot here is that AA uses a fixed award chart for partner bookings rather than dynamic pricing, so the cost is predictable: typically 70,000 miles one-way in business class from the US to the Middle East. Compare this to AA's own Flagship Business product on the same routes (which often prices at 60,000-85,000 miles with dynamic pricing) and you are getting a dramatically superior product — QSuites — for a comparable or lower mileage cost. AA does not impose fuel surcharges on partner awards, keeping out-of-pocket costs to taxes and fees only.

Let's run the numbers on a concrete example.

The Route: Washington Dulles (IAD) to Doha (DOH) on Qatar Airways QR 22, operating a Boeing 777-300ER with QSuites. This is a nonstop flight of approximately 13 hours — exactly the kind of long-haul journey where your seat product matters enormously.

The Cash Price: A business class ticket on this route typically runs $5,500 to $7,500, and during peak travel windows — think spring break, summer, or major holidays — it can reach $9,000. Call it a realistic average of $6,500.

The Points Cost: 70,000 AAdvantage miles + approximately $80–$120 in taxes and fees.

The Math: At $6,500 cash value against 70,000 miles, you're getting 9.3 cents per point. Against a $9,000 peak ticket, you're at 12.9 cents per point. Either way, this is among the highest-value AAdvantage redemptions available anywhere in the program.

You arrive at Dulles and proceed to the Qatar Airways check-in counter, where you're processed as a business class passenger. At Doha, you'll have access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge — one of the most celebrated airport lounges in the world, featuring a full à la carte restaurant, shower suites, and a calm, spacious environment that makes a layover feel genuinely pleasant.

Onboard, your QSuite is a private cabin with a door that slides closed. The bed extends to a full 80 inches. You'll be offered a genuine dine-on-demand service — no scheduled meal times, no "chicken or pasta" announcements over the intercom. The wine list is serious. The bedding is from The White Company. The 21.5-inch screen is 4K.

For the ChooseFI community, the most powerful part of this isn't the luxury itself — it's the ratio. You're experiencing a $6,500–$9,000 product for the cost of points you earned on everyday spending and a small tax outlay. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: maximum experience per dollar (or point) deployed.

Do this: Book as far out as possible. AAdvantage allows bookings up to 331 days in advance. Qatar releases its best award inventory to partner programs at the time of schedule opening — not closer to departure. If you have a target travel window, search at the 331-day mark. Availability genuinely deteriorates as departure approaches.

Do this: Watch for Web Special pricing drops. AAdvantage's Web Specials have historically offered Qatar business class awards at 50,000 miles instead of the standard 70,000. These appear without warning on aa.com under the "Web Specials" tab. If you're flexible with your dates within a week or two, checking this section regularly (or signing up for AAdvantage email alerts) can save you 20,000 miles — a meaningful difference.

Do this: Use Citi ThankYou for same-day transfers. If you find award space and need to transfer points immediately, Citi ThankYou → AAdvantage transfers are instant. This is the fastest transfer path and eliminates the risk of space disappearing while your transfer processes. Keep Citi points in reserve as your QSuites "strike fund."

Avoid this: Transferring Marriott points unless absolutely necessary. The Marriott Bonvoy → AAdvantage transfer at 3:1 is deeply inefficient. You're spending three Marriott points to create one AAdvantage mile. Marriott points are worth roughly 0.7–0.8 cents each, meaning you're paying effectively 2.1–2.4 cents per AAdvantage mile — still potentially worth it for QSuites, but exhaust your Citi and Bilt options first.

Do this: Treat DOH as a hub, not a destination. Doha is Qatar's base, meaning a 70,000-mile award from the US to DOH can be the first leg of an onward journey to destinations across Asia, South Asia, or East Africa — all on Qatar metal. A trip from IAD to Singapore (SIN) routing through DOH, for example, puts you in QSuites for the transatlantic leg and potentially a narrowbody for the shorter DOH-SIN segment.

Avoid this: Booking round-trip when one-way is more flexible. AAdvantage allows one-way partner awards. Book your outbound and return separately — this dramatically expands your availability options and lets you mix partners or return on a different airline without being locked into a single itinerary.

Do this: Build AAdvantage miles through Bilt's monthly rent payments. Bilt Rewards is the only major program that earns points on rent. If you're paying $1,500–$2,500/month in rent, a year of Bilt earning generates 18,000–30,000 Bilt points — transferable to AAdvantage at 1:1. That's a meaningful contribution to your 70,000-mile target from a spend category you have anyway.

This redemption is purpose-built for the serious couple or solo traveler with a specific long-haul itinerary in mind — a honeymoon, a milestone anniversary trip, a once-in-a-while splurge that you've decided to fund with points rather than cash. If your travel goal is experiencing a world-class business class product nearly free, this is among the best vehicles in the entire points ecosystem.

Minimum requirements: 70,000 AAdvantage miles per person, plus $80–$150 in cash for taxes and fees. You also need the patience and flexibility to find saver award space, which is the primary friction in this redemption.

## Honest Difficulty Assessment: Moderate This redemption scores **moderate difficulty** — and that rating is accurate. It's not a click-and-book process like domestic awards, but it's not the multi-step puzzle that some ultra-premium redemptions require either. The difficulty is concentrated in **two specific areas**. **Challenge #1: Finding Available Award Space** Qatar releases QSuites award inventory to AAdvantage, but not generously. Availability scores a **2 out of 5**, which means you will sometimes search for weeks before finding the right date. This is the primary bottleneck. The fix: search early (331 days out), be flexible within a 1-2 week window, and use ExpertFlyer alerts to get notified when space opens. Midweek departures and shoulder-season travel windows (late January through March, September through November) tend to surface more space. **Challenge #2: Building 70,000 AAdvantage Miles** AAdvantage's transfer partner list is narrower than Chase or Amex ecosystems. Your best paths are Citi ThankYou (instant transfers) and Bilt Rewards (1-2 days). This earns a **3 out of 5** for ease of earning — achievable, but requires intentional card strategy rather than casual accumulation. **The booking process itself** — once you have miles and availability — is straightforward on aa.com. AAdvantage's award search tool clearly displays partner availability and pricing. **The encouragement:** Every traveler in the ChooseFI community who has navigated this redemption consistently describes it as worth every minute of the search process. The moment that QSuite door closes, you'll understand exactly why. If you're willing to invest the time to find availability and build your miles intentionally, this redemption is entirely within reach — and the payoff is extraordinary.

Log into your AAdvantage account and search for one-way business class flights on your desired route. Filter for partner-operated flights and look specifically for Qatar Airways (QR) flight numbers. The search results will show the mileage cost alongside availability.

If aa.com does not show availability, search the same route on Qatar's own website using a Privilege Club account. Qatar sometimes releases space that AA's system takes 24-48 hours to reflect. If you find space on Qatar but not AA, check back the following day.

Not all Qatar business class flights operate QSuites. Check the aircraft type listed in the search results — A350-1000 and select 777-300ERs have QSuites. Verify on SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to ensure you are booking the premium product.

Once you confirm QSuites availability, complete the booking on aa.com using your AAdvantage miles. The process is the same as booking any AA award flight. You will see the mileage cost plus taxes and fees before confirming.

American Airlines charges approximately 70,000 AAdvantage miles one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights. Taxes and fees are typically $30 to $80. A round trip comes to roughly 140,000 miles total plus minimal fees.

Both options cost roughly 70,000 points one-way. The main differences are earning sources and booking experience. AAdvantage miles are earned through Citi cards and Bilt, while Avios can be earned through Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt. AA offers web booking while BA may require phone calls. Check availability through both programs — they sometimes see different award space.

Yes. The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select earns bonus miles on purchases, Bilt Rewards transfers to AAdvantage at 1:1, AA's SimplyMiles program earns miles on everyday purchases linked to your credit card, and the AAdvantage shopping portal earns miles at online retailers. You can accumulate 70,000 or more miles without taking a single AA flight.

Airlines control how much award inventory they release to each partner. Qatar may release seats to BA's Avios program but not to AA, or vice versa. AA's search engine also has known inconsistencies with partner availability display. Always cross-reference qatarairways.com and ba.com if aa.com shows no availability on your desired dates.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using AAdvantage miles for Qatar business class is one of the strongest partner award redemptions in the oneworld alliance. At 70,000 miles for a product that retails at $5,000 to $8,000, the value per mile is outstanding. The web-based booking experience on aa.com removes the friction of phone calls, and the lack of fuel surcharges keeps your cash outlay minimal. If you earn AAdvantage miles through Citi cards or Bilt transfers, this should be at the top of your aspirational redemption list. #9119. Foster + Partners creates Area worktable for today's office

Foster + Partners Industrial Design aimed to bring expressive and functional workplace design together in its modular Area table system, created with Spanish furniture brand Kettal.

Designed to be durable and adaptable, Area combines aluminium columns, a panoply of tabletop options and concealed power.

The aluminium columns anchor the design, serving as both structural support and discreet container for power cables and electrical components.

Available in three diameters – 90, 160 or 450 millimetres – and either anodised or powder-coated finishes, they also bring customisable personality to the worktable.

The tabletops, meanwhile, come in shapes ranging from round to triangular and rhomboid and materials including timber, linoleum, melamine and Fenix. For larger conference or feature tables, terrazzo or marble are also options.

“Area is a collection of durable, expressive elements that define workstations and gathering points within a space to support both individual and collaborative work,” said Foster + Partners head of industrial design Mike Holland.

“The development of Area involved finding the right balance between structural performance, flexibility and visual simplicity,” he continued.

“The system needed to accommodate a wide variety of tabletop configurations and working arrangements, while integrating the technical infrastructure required in contemporary workplaces.”

The Area system can be accessorised with lighting or fabric screen dividers, the infrastructure for which is built into the table. Screen dividers attach magnetically at designed points, with lighting used in combination or mounted independently.

Cables are hidden underneath the tabletop within a J-profile aluminium beam that also provides structural support, while concealed grommets provide access to plug sockets and USB-C connections.

Holland told Dezeen that designing these accessories so they could function seamlessly across a range of tabletop configurations was the key challenge of the design process for Area, alongside achieving the desired proportions and textures for the aluminium columns.

To realise their vision for the expansive system, the design team undertook extensive prototyping, including using both one-to-one and full-scale models and augmented reality (AR).

“Working with full-scale models, augmented reality and 3D printing allowed us to understand the relationship between the different components and how they would function together in real working environments,” said Holland.

“This approach was particularly important in refining the columns, assessing their proportions, and adapting the surface texture pattern at full scale. It also allowed us to evolve the design from wider diameters into more elegant and efficient forms.”

He said that working with models and AR also allowed manufacturer Kettal to engage in the design process and contribute ideas.

“Collaboration is at the heart of our approach, and we believe it is fundamental to achieving the highest-quality results,” said Holland.

Area was designed for the contemporary workplace, said Holland, where flexible and hybrid working have made the office primarily a place for collaboration and connection, and where the table’s modularity and adaptability allow it to evolve as needs change.

“As designers, we are interested in the points of interaction between people and buildings,” said Holland. “At the heart of industrial design lies the creation of these touchpoints through which people experience space.”

“In the workplace, furniture plays a vital role in shaping how people engage with their environment, influencing how they occupy, navigate and connect with the spaces around them,” Holland concluded.

Part of the architecture firm Foster + Partners, Foster + Partners Industrial Design started by creating site-specific furniture, fixtures and fittings for the company’s buildings and over the last 50 years have expanded to more stand-alone commercial products.

Some of its recent designs include the Join plywood furniture collection, Ori bird feeders and Datum porcelain tableware.

#9118. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#9116. In Sammy Baloji’s Hands, ‘Objective’ Materials Reveal New Truths About African History

In the mid-2000s, after he completed his master’s degree in information sciences and communication at the University of Lubumbashi, Sammy Baloji started working with the French Institute. The director of the institute, also based in Lubumbashi, was interested in colonial architecture and cultural heritage history, and he collaborated with academics researching those topics.

Baloji’s work for the French Institute mainly entailed photographing events and later working with researchers from France. But he was already on the way to becoming the artist he is today. Related Articles Actor Says He Removed His Mother's Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest French Artist Claude Lévêque Ordered to Stand Trial for Rape and Sexual Assault of Minors

Working at the French Institute, he recalled in an interview with ARTnews, “really shifted my perspective, in terms of outlining photography or research, because I was interested in the way that [the researchers] were addressing the city or buildings or cultural heritage from a historical and objective perspective. I was mainly interested in people’s experiences, the testimonies of people who are living [in Lubumbashi like] myself.”

The two opposite approaches opened up the question of how he could “use the so-called scientific objective materials and bring them close to the human experience, to the architecture of local sites.”

The inquiry led the artist to make one of his first significant projects, Mémoire (2006), a photography collage series of colonial-era black and white archival images and colored prints showing contemporary Lubumbashi in the Katanga province, which is rich in mineral resources including copper, uranium, lithium, diamonds and cobalt.

Baloji’s work for the French Institute had allowed him to observe the social, environmental and political impact of mining in Katanga. Now, using a combination of photography and research, he was able to underscore how Belgian colonization had shaped the Democratic Republic of Congo, whose history of extraction he has continued to explore.

Works continuing to build on the themes of Mémoire can currently be seen in two high-profile showings. Baloji is making his debut US solo with “When Extraction Becomes Form It Speaks In Borrowed Tongues,” at the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio, on view through February 14, 2027. The exhibition explores how Europe’s decorative arts and architecture still include elements of Congo’s colonialist history and the extraction of natural resources. It takes a critical look at the impact on land, people and cultural forms, speaking to complicated relationships between Central Africa, Europe, and the Americas.

Concurrently with the Wexner Center show, Baloji’s work can be seen at the Venice Biennale, both in the main show, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, and in the national pavilion of the Democratic Republic of Congo. In the main exhibition at Venice, Baloji is showing three sculptures and 16 collage prints. Two of the sculptures reference works from a 19th-century Belgian colonial museum and the national collection built in the 1970s by the former President of the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mobutu Sese Seko.

“I started to realize that the colonial system was not just about controlling territory but also occupying societies and imposing new rules,” said Baloji, who splits his time between Brussels and Lubumbashi.

In the Wexner show, Baloji is exhibiting Suspension (Debris of History, Matters of Memory), a commission conceived with architect Gloria Cabral and in collaboration with art historian Cécile Fromont. Drawing from the design of historical Kongo cloth, the suspended large-scale sculpture is made of mining and construction waste, the latter from recent work at the Wexner Center. Meanwhile, a new tapestry called Rethreaded Indies, made by Baloji and Fromont, addresses the French Old Indies tapestry series (1637–1730), produced at the royal Gobelins manufactory in Paris, connecting that with Kongolese weaving. The works use textile and architecture to correct misinformation about African histories, showing how European colonization has shaped the continent’s narratives, often for the worse.

“I would say my interest in his work is how he weaves these histories together, and in a way that I find extremely compelling,” said Julieta González, the head of visual arts at the Wexner Center and the curator of the artist’s exhibition. Baloji’s work, she added, “is important because it weaves together so many historical events and situations but with materiality that speaks to the particular situation he’s critiquing, which is the legacies of colonialism” in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The show she curated, she said, offers the public “an insight into [the artist’s] very research-oriented practice and how it unfolds in so many different mediums [which includes] video, sculpture and photography.”

Baloji was born in 1978 in Lubumbashi and grew up with, in some sense, limited knowledge about the history of Belgium’s colonization of the Democratic Republic of Congo. (Connecting that and resource extraction in Katanga with global or political history came later following reports of Congo supplying Iran with uranium, which the Central African country denied.) In secondary school, Baloji cofounded a collective that read and shared books from libraries and schools that they had access to. He was also drawing at the time, producing some of his first artworks.

His parents did not encourage his plan to study at the Fine Art Academy, so for his master’s degree, he studied information sciences and communication, which happened to align with the artistic practices he was interested in. Ironically, or maybe coincidentally, the course Baloji pursued to appease his parents so he could make his own career choices ended up being formative to his practice.

Baloji is also known for more than just his art. In 2008, he cofounded the Lubumbashi-based Picha Art and Research Center and the Lubumbashi Biennale, whose ninth edition, cocurated by Congolese-Belgian curator Sorana Munsya and Ethiopian-Eritrean-Italian artist Jermay Michael Gabriel, opened in October. The art space and biennial are platforms that help expand access to the arts and support local artists with needed infrastructure, especially because of limited state support.

Camille Ostermann, an independent art consultant who worked on Congo’s national pavilion at the Venice Biennale, said, “I’ve admired [Baloji’s] collaborative practice [since the early 2010s]: works co-authored with historians, exhibitions built around artists he invites. But it was at the Lubumbashi Biennale, which Picha organizes, that I saw this spirit at work. In a city shaped by mining, by what is extracted and carried elsewhere, Picha does the opposite: it builds, gathers, gives back. Many artists told me their paths had been changed by Picha and Sammy’s mentorship. Like Ibrahim Mahama in Tamale or Yinka Shonibare in Lagos, Sammy works internationally while staying rooted in Lubumbashi, deliberately keeping the two connected: what he builds abroad can open doors for others at home.”

Picha Center and the Lubumbashi Biennale are also, in some ways, an extension of Baloji’s research and practice. The biennial, he said, can start conversations about extractivism and ecological crisis, as well as talk about “the impact of international and economic interests on the environment and societies.” It was a statement that could easily have been applied to many of his artworks.

#9115. Pepper & Well designs bathroom that mimics concrete architecture of Paul Couch house

Melbourne-based studio Pepper & Well took cues from crisscrossing concrete walls and ceiling beams when designing Lumeah, a new en-suite for a house by celebrated architect Paul Couch.

Located in Macedon, central Victoria, the linear single-storey house was completed in 2006 by the late Couch, who passed away earlier this year.

When new owners bought the property in 2018, they felt the layout and finishes of the main bathroom didn’t meet the standards of the rest of the house.

They asked Pepper & Well to upgrade it and make it more accessible.

“There was an opportunity to make the space more comfortable and practical as they aged,” said lead architect Andy Dal Pozzo.

The previous layout included a WC, an enclosed shower and a step-in plunge pool, all within a space just 3.5 metres long.

Pepper & Well’s scheme removed the plunge, allowing space for a larger WC and for an open shower to be built in place of the old frosted-glass enclosure.

The defining move was the addition of a cast-concrete element that partitions the toilet and shower areas.

This incorporates an informal bench, allowing for seated showers if preferred.

The geometry of this element clearly references the house’s exposed concrete structure, a rhythmic arrangement of concrete beams over concrete walls.

“Our approach began with understanding the logic of Paul’s work,” explained Dal Pozzo.

“We wanted the renovation to share the original architecture’s material honesty and clarity, while remaining recognisable as a new contribution,” he said.

A change in floor surface marks the junction between old and new.

While most of the room features the bluestone flooring installed 20 years ago, the toilet and shower have a surface of crazy-paved slate.

The stone is the same Mintaro Brown Back slate that Couch installed in the bathroom of his own house, Toolern Vale.

“Laid in crazy paving beside the retained bluestone, it introduces a distinct texture with a direct connection to Paul’s work,” said Dal Pozzo.

The rest of the room was left largely intact, including the solid timber doors and the vanity unit spanning the opposite wall.

There are subtle correlations between the two sides of the room, so as not to make the new insertion feel disparate. For instance, a glass screen matches the height of the mirror opposite.

The shower also includes a stainless-steel handrail that doubles as a towel rail, matching the rest of the bathroom fixtures.

“The scale of the commission demanded close attention to every decision, from the arrangement of the room to the meeting of two stones,” added Dal Pozzo.

“By revealing the original fabric, retaining what worked and introducing a few carefully resolved elements, we sought to give the clients a bathroom that would serve them into the future and continue the architectural story of their home.”

Lumeah is shortlisted for bathroom of the year in Dezeen Awards 2026.

Other projects in this category include Kan Atelier’s design for the William King Apartment, a residence in a 1950s block in Athens, which won the public vote.

#9114. Ron Howard on Telling Richard Avedon’s ‘Very Human Story’ in New Netflix Doc

By Brande Victorian for The Hollywood Reporter

Ron Howard knows his way around a camera: in front of and behind the lens; scripted film or documentary feature. But when his production company, Imagine Entertainment (co-chaired by Brian Grazer), was considering a biodoc on fashion photographer Richard Avedon, Howard wasn’t sure if he should be at the helm.

“I really went into it thinking, ‘This is a great subject, it’d be great for Imagine,’” Howard said of the Avedon Foundation opening up the artist’s archives to him during a screening at SCAD Film Festival on Oct. 28. “As I began sort of seeing the breadth of that work, I was immediately impressed, but I still felt like, I’m not sure I’m really the right filmmaker for this, but this is fascinating and I bet we could explore what went on behind the scenes making many of these great photos that we remember.” Related Articles New Richard Avedon Documentary Shows That Fashion Isn't All Style--It's Substance, Too Netflix Acquires Richard Avedon Documentary for 2026 Release After Cannes Debut

“As I began to do some research, soon I really did connect with it as this very human story that I wanted to tell,” Howard continued. “It was less anecdotal about how photos were done and what glamorous or intriguing figures sat for him, and much, much more about an artist’s journey, and I related to it. In some ways, we’re very different people—he’s an extrovert, I’m not; he was the life of the party, I avoid them—but, man, did he have drive and ambition.”

The resulting film, Avedon, now streaming on Netflix, blends commentary from collaborators—former magazine editor Tina Brown, model Lauren Hutton and dancer and choreographer Twyla Tharp—with Richard’s works, both commercial and historic, like his portraits of figures of the civil rights movement. The project heavily explores Avedon’s legacy as an artist with strong creative and political convictions, as well as his struggle balancing those passions with his obligations as a husband and father.

“Ultimately, we had 500 photographs in the documentary, but our amazing producing partner, Dallas Brennan Rexer, combed through 16,000 sittings of Avedon,” producer Sara Bernstein, president of Imagine Documentaries, explained during the Q&A. “Initially, we thought there might be a select number of hero images that would take us through Avedon’s creative story. But then there’s this backdrop of, essentially, the back half of the 20th century, so you could match these images with these different moments in history or these different personalities who represent different buckets of history. And then you were able to see a deeper, personal story when John Avedon sat down for us.”

Richard’s son, John, whose son, Michael, is also a fashion photographer, was a “reluctant interview,” despite being supportive of the project, Howard noted as he shared how he got John on board as a talking head.“Frankly, I said to him, ‘There’s a gap here because we have your father’s voice. We have people who worked with him, but we don’t have that intimate connection, that deeper understanding that’s away from the studio.’ And I think as a writer himself, he recognized that there was a role for him to fill,” said Howard, later adding, “now [the film] became a generational thing about fathers and sons in addition to everything else.”In one of the final scenes of the film, Avedon, who died in 2001, makes a startlingly reticent prediction about the outlook on his art form, stating, “I don’t think there will be photography in the future, only machines.”Asked what he thinks Avedon would capture at this moment in time, where the battle between art and AI seems to be reaching its peak, Howard said, “He’d probably still be shooting on the white paper and probably still using that three-by-five camera because, for him, it did become a kind of communication and an exploration, capturing those moments. I think he would still be entirely relevant because he became the story behind the story as an artist. And we began to recognize his work; whether we knew it was Avedon, we could feel the hand of a creator.”

Added Howard of how Richard might approach AI, “My guess is also with his sensibility and aesthetic, he’d be using it as a tool to advance his aesthetic. I don’t think he’d be necessarily running away from it, but he would want to stay in control.”
