#9083. inside ava roth’s artistic collaboration with thousands of tiny bee workers

from encaustic painting to interspecies sculpture, ava roth's work draws on bees, natural materials and the possibilities of collaborative making

annalise kamegawa November 19, 2026 8 min

One of Ava Roth’s most valuable collaborators is not human. In fact, it’s the bees. In her series, Kintsu-Bee, she places broken ceramics into a hive of bees who, through the formation of honeycombs, create a new bond between the cracked pieces. The method is named after the Japanese repair method, kintsugi, which uses lacquer and gold leaf to create a shining new seam in broken dishware, turning what was once considered waste into a valuable new form. From this, Roth’s work expands beyond cups and plates. She has experimented with frames, textiles, and even embroidery hoops to create structures in collaboration with the planet’s busiest insects. In this extraordinary interspecies project, the Canadian artist and artisan creates a powerful meditation on the power of the natural world, craft, and more-than-human intelligence. Her work has gone on to be recognized by Homo Faber and has been exhibited internationally, including in Canada, where she’s from.

In conversation with designboom, artist Ava Roth shares what brought her to the hives, her multimedia works, and her relationship with the bees. She says of her process, ‘I am committed to sharing the labor equally, meaning that in each piece I try to give as much of my own time and effort as I am hoping the bees will offer.’

Kintsugi/Kintsu-Bee Cup #1 ceramic plate by Satoshi Yoshikawa and natural honeycomb | all images courtesy of Ava RothCherry Beach Salvage on Paper Salvaged garbage, rocks, encaustic medium, paper, wire and natural honeycomb

Famed American poet Emily Dickinson wrote in To make a prairie (1779), one of her poems about bees, ‘To make a prairie it takes a clover and one bee,/ One clover, and a bee./ And revery.’ In this musing on the creation of plains, the wonder bees can inspire comes to life. From their essential role as a pollinator species to their intricate hexagonal combs and the sweet honey they produce, bees are not only invaluable to the functions of the natural world, but the complex worlds they create in their hives continue to inspire artists.

Seeing their value as a keystone species, one that’s critical to the greater functioning of their environment, has inspired many artists like Roth. For example, Pierre Huyghe’s Untilled (Liegender Frauenakt) [Reclining Female Nude] (2012) features an actively maintained beehive atop a human body and is held in the collections of MoMA in New York. In this sculpture, the artist comments on the collective thinking capacity of bees. There’s also the work of Pollinator Pathmaker by Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg, which seeks to bring pollinating species back to specified regions through an algorithmically generated plot of pollinator-optimized plants. These works, just a few in a world of bee-forward art, show how the insects have inspired creatives both with their incredible intelligence and their importance to the cycles of the environment.

One form of art particularly linked to the legacy of bees is encaustic painting. Using a mixture of melted, pigmented beeswax and resin, an artist can build pigmented layers similar to those of an oil painter. ‘I was working with encaustic as my primary media,’ Roth says of the technique. Some of these works incorporate the golden ginkgo leaf and embroidery floss, while others feature horsehair and photographs of expansive bodies of water. ‘Being immersed in wax naturally led to a curiosity about bees. And the more I learned about bees, the more that knowledge began to inform my work, which in turn led me to take a beekeeping course. During this period of learning, I found myself incorporating pieces of burr comb into my work and building encaustic paintings inside hive frames.’

After working with encaustics, Roth notes that her next big leap was training with Master Beekeeper Mylee Nordin. On this experience, she notes, ‘Her expertise and oversight provided me with the confidence to keep an apiary in my backyard. At that point, the final move to putting my work directly into hives was almost inevitable!’ She points out that this body of work wasn’t the intention. It was more, what she calls, ‘a process of playful experimentation born out of genuine curiosity and deep respect,’ for her insect collaborators.

As a multimedia artist, much like in her work with encaustics, Roth’s bee sculptures start with an arrangement of embroidery, paintings, photographs, and other materials. When creating these structures, she works with space in mind for the honeycombs and other alterations that will eventually occur once they’re placed in the hive. ‘Control is also something I try hard to share equally,’ she says of the collaborative nature of her work. ‘Importantly, I don’t force the bees to engage with the art in any way. In other words, whether or not the bees build their comb on any given piece, let alone how much and in what shapes, is left entirely to them.’

After Roth creates this structure, it’s up to the bees to finalize the form. Though the structure of a comb is fairly regular in shape and color, Roth admits that ‘Most of the pieces surprise [her] in some way, which is one of the great delights of this project.’ She highlights two pieces in particular: ‘One was a two-dimensional beaded piece that, for some reason that is beyond me, the bees built a massive and undulating armature of comb over. The structure of the comb is really gorgeous, much more complex and massive than on anything else I’ve seen in the decade I’ve been working on this project. Another is a small piece of driftwood and knitted wire, where the bees collectively decided to trace and mimic the pattern of the wire with their comb, which is truly remarkable.’

Inherent in Roth’s work is a juxtaposition between the man-made and the forces of nature. Through these small meditations on the logic of bees, their combs bulging, bonding, and restructuring her objects, she sheds light on how the intelligence of these little insects is at once comparable to our own and entirely beyond our comprehension. Yet, rather than attempting to understand or control this intelligence, Roth makes space for it to unfold. Her work asks us to reconsider what it means to create, and whether art-making must remain an exclusively human act. By sharing both the labor and the authorship with her bees, Roth offers a different model of artistic collaboration, one rooted in patience, reciprocity, and respect for the natural world.

Roth says she continually finds herself amazed by the creation of the beesher work asks us to reconsider what it means to create, and whether art-making must remain an exclusively human act

#9082. Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year

Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.

Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.

Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.

London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Read more about the Designers of the Year below:

Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet.

Ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.

“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” said the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo

Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.

“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”

Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.

His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.

Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.

“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”

Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.

Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.

Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem

Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.

“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.

“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.

Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.

Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.

“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.

He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.

I test out the very best audiophile wired headphones for a living and out of all of them, the best open-back option is hands down the HEDDphone D1. And even at its original price of £599, it's worth every penny.

But thanks to this early Black Friday headphone deal, the HEDDphone D1 is now down from £599 to £499 over at Peter Tyson.

Open-back headphones are the holy grail for audiophiles craving a spacious soundstage, but they usually offer some unique hurdles to achieve true tonal accuracy. When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I said that the German audio company had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

Sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

If you do get the HEDDphone D1 it's worth getting a quality headphone stand too. And you really don't have to spend loads of money to get a good-quality, handsome, wooden stand. For me a good option is the Linkidea wooden stand. Even when it's not discounted, under £30 is a bargain.

Usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

At 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.

This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

#9080. What Does Dark Green Poop Mean? Causes, Diet, and When to See a Doctor

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Bum nuggets typically sport a classic brown, so glancing back into the loo and spying on greenish-colored poop can throw you for a loop.

Most of the time, green poop reflects a leafy diet or your body’s unique way of breaking things down. But if the green becomes a recurring (fecal) matter, it might be something else.

Continue reading to learn more about poop color, its meaning, and when it’s time to make an appointment with a healthcare provider.

Spotting green or another unexpected color in the toilet can be startling, but it’s more common than you might think. From dietary influences to your body’s digestion speed, several factors can change poop from earthy tones to other shades. Let’s check some out.

Are you chowing down on lots of green leafy veggies like spinach, kale, or broccoli? These foods are high in chlorophyll, which can dye your doodles green. Chlorophyll doesn’t always break down entirely before reaching your intestines, meaning it passes through your system and colors your stool green.

Have you ever had a St. Paddy’s Day-themed milkshake or a brightly colored cake? Artificial colors in foods and drinks can change poop from brown to green. It’s not magic! It’s just the dye in green food passing through your gut unchanged.

When your digestive system processes food too rapidly, it doesn’t allow for the full breakdown of bile, a yellow-green fluid that aids digestion. This often results in a greenish stool, especially during fast-moving episodes of diarrhea.

Have you recently been taking antibiotics? These meds can reset your gut’s bacterial crew. Since these tiny critters play a big part in the shade of your stool, introducing antibiotics might cause green poop sometimes.

If you’ve had certain medical treatments, it can affect digestion and cause bright green poop. One example is graft-versus-host disease, which may occur with bone marrow transplants. This tricky condition can bring about less-than-welcome guests, like diarrhea and green stool. It’s a clear signal from your body that things are out of sync.

Some uninvited microscopic guests like Salmonella bacteria, the water-loving mini parasite Giardia, and norovirus can also be a reason for your poop turning green. These critters can hustle your digestion at an unnaturally quick pace, turning your stool green as they disrupt your gut’s usual rhythm.

Babies can surprise you with a whole crayon box of poop colors, and green is definitely in the mix.

For infants, green stool might stem from the same factors as adults, like dietary changes. This includes adjustments when they start eating solids or changes in a parent’s diet if chestfeeding.

Another harmless cause could be ingesting a small amount of amniotic fluid in the womb. So, if you notice your little one sporting some spring grass-colored diapers, it’s usually no biggie.

If the green theme park in your toilet isn’t closing down, or if it’s accompanied by other symptoms like severe stomach pain, nausea, or diarrhea, it might be time to call in the pros. Persistent changes in stool color may signal underlying health issues that need medical attention.

Dark green poop can result from eating lots of leafy greens or foods with green coloring. However, it can also indicate that food travels quickly through the digestive system.

While liver issues can change stool color, they usually turn it pale or dark, not green. If you’re worried about liver health, look for pale or clay-colored stools instead.

If you haven’t been on a kale-eating spree, dark green poop might be from iron supplements or constipation remedies, which can also give poop a greenish tint.

Dark poop could be a sign of your diet or medications. However, if it’s black and tar-like, it might mean bleeding in your upper gastrointestinal tract. In that case, chatting with a healthcare professional is a must.

While green poop can def throw you through a loop, it’s usually not a sign of anything serious. It’s often your body’s way of dealing with what you eat or how fast you digest. So, unless it’s paired with other worrying symptoms, there’s probably no need to panic.

Last medically reviewed on August 2, 2024

#9079. corrugated metal and sawtooth roofs wrap occupational center in northern portugal

an inclusive occupational center for disabled people in vila nova de paiva, designed by salto studio, explores the psychological potential of a building’s iconography.

André Nave edited by christina vergopoulou November 20, 2026 3 min

Located in Vila Nova de Paiva in northern Portugal, CACI 5.3.8 is an occupational center for people with disabilities designed by Salto Studio. Named after its five elevations, three primary rooms, and eight roof ridges, the facility draws on the typology of industrial workshops, framed around the concept of a ‘dream factory,’ to establish a workplace-like environment for daily activities. To reconcile a sloped site while maintaining universal accessibility, the volume is slightly elevated to keep the entire interior on a single, continuous level, enabling step-free circulation from the higher northern grade to adjacent complex structures, including an existing care home. Within the compact footprint, carved-out patios and planted pockets bring direct and indirect daylight, natural ventilation, and landscape views deep into the floor plan while supporting outdoor programming.

For the layout, Salto Studio organizes four distinct volumes around a central lobby that connects three primary programmatic spaces: an activities room for making, a dining room for eating, and a living room for socializing. Each room features a distinct plan geometry, ceiling height, and solar orientation calibrated to its specific function. Above, a steel-frame structural system supports sawtooth roofs that reference industrial studio architecture. Addressing a tight construction schedule and budget, the metal skeleton is clad in corrugated insulated metal panels arranged in varying rhythms according to building height. Inside, mineral-fiber acoustic ceiling panels and linoleum flooring regulate sound levels, while all-electric heat pumps, photovoltaic arrays, and reused on-site exterior paving eliminate fossil fuel reliance and reduce construction waste.

#9078. Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

#9075. Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” said Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”

Xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.

#9074. Construction underway on Jean Nouvel's landmark opera house in China

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped plan, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included BIG, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

#9073. james turrell fills new york gallery with floating cubes and glowing walls of light

the legendary light artist brings floating cubes and luminous walls to almine rech's tribeca gallery in new york.

James Turrell has filled Almine Rech’s Tribeca gallery in New York with luminous forms that seem to extend from the walls and hover in midair. Titled Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue, the exhibition brings together over fifteen works, and even includes new installations that revisit some of the artist’s earliest experiments with light and perception.

A rectangular opening glows violet against a darkened wall. Elsewhere, a luminous cube appears to float where two walls meet, with its sharp edges suggesting a solid object suspended in space. The room itself becomes difficult to read as the light alters viewers’ sense of depth and distance.

The show is on view through January 30th, 2027, and marks Turrell’s first presentation with Almine Rech in the United States. It arrives nearly four decades after their first collaboration in Paris, and returns to ideas that have occupied the artist since the 1960s.

Among the new works is the installation Shallow Space, part of a series in which James Turrell uses illuminated apertures to create unexpected depth within a wall. At first, the luminous surface can appear completely flat, like a field of color. As the viewer’s eyes adjust, the opening reveals an actual space beyond the wall, although its dimensions remain difficult to judge.

In Raemar II (2026), a glowing rectangular form casts violet light across the surrounding surfaces. Color spreads beyond its edges and gradually dissolves into the room. From a distance, the work resembles an illuminated painting, although its relationship to the wall is far more ambiguous.

The exhibition also introduces new pieces from the artist‘s Glassworks series, which uses precisely programmed LEDs behind etched glass. Colors change gradually across these luminous surfaces, and the apparent depth of each work shifts with them. Some passages of light appear dense and opaque, while others seem to recede far beyond the physical dimensions of the piece.

Another new installation, Afrum Violet (2026), returns to James Turrell’s Cross Corner projections. A sharply defined violet form occupies the intersection of two walls, where the geometry of the room helps create the illusion of a three-dimensional cube. The surrounding surfaces absorb a softer wash of purple, while the central form retains its remarkably precise edges.

Turrell began experimenting with these projections in 1966 at the former Mendota Hotel in Ocean Park, California, where he converted the building into a studio. By directing light onto the walls at specific angles, he discovered that a simple projection could appear to have weight and volume. A shape formed by light could become surprisingly convincing as a physical presence.

Six decades later, the strange effect remains. From one spot, the illuminated planes read as a solid cube. Move through the room, and the relationship between the shape and its architectural setting begins to change. The installation asks viewers to spend time with something as familiar as a corner and reconsider exactly what they are seeing.

#9072. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#9071. SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor plan of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely new”, SSdH said.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, said SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio said.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

8BitDo’s Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Ultimate 3 and Pro 3 are collectables you’ll actually want to use, and the unboxing alone is a treat.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

The controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

The metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

Then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

What's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

The less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

This is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

But I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

Switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

#9069. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

#9068. marguerite humeau discusses myth-making, spirituality and our connection to other forms of life

the artist reflects on how animal intelligence, ancient rituals and alternative forms of knowledge can expand our understanding of life beyond the human.

‘Extinction doesn’t necessarily only happen to bodies,’ Marguerite Humeau tells designboom during our interview. ‘We can also think about the extinction of mental landscapes and imagination.’ It is a thought that has come to shape the French artist’s practice, which moves between prehistoric life, ancient civilizations, animal intelligence and speculative futures. Through sculpture and installation, Humeau gives form to worlds that cannot be fully known, drawing on scientific research, historical accounts, mythology and forms of knowledge that sit beyond conventional disciplines.

For around 15 years, she has been interested in bringing lost lives and forgotten worlds back into view. Her early work involved resuscitating extinct bodies through imagined prehistoric creatures, before she turned to the voice of Cleopatra in Echoes (2015). The project marked a shift in her thinking. Looking for connections between ancient Egypt and contemporary attitudes toward life and death, she began to see myth-making as a central part of her practice. ‘I was trying to understand their essence, and explore whether they have parallels with our own times and how they can still help us understand the world today,’ the artist explains.

Her interest in the stories humans create to make sense of existence continues to run through her work, although its protagonists have moved beyond humanity. In FOXP2, Humeau imagined an alternate evolutionary history in which elephants, rather than humans, had developed civilization. The project opened up a longer investigation into animal rituals and parallel forms of presence, continued through Mist, High Tide, and her work for the Venice Biennale in 2022. She began speculating that mass death in the animal world might give rise to new forms of spirituality and ritual among other species.

The artist’s research has also returned to the earliest stages of human experience. In Ecstasies, she recreated an imagined early trance, considering the possibility that such an experience marked the moment when humans first sensed realities beyond what they could physically perceive. Across these projects, she is drawn to the threshold between what can be explained and what remains mysterious. ‘We’re human, and we’re longing for mystery and transcendence. We want to become part of something bigger than ourselves,’ she shares with us.

After years spent imagining ancient and future worlds, during the pandemic Humeau became interested in the unfamiliar ecosystems already existing beneath the ground. ‘There were actually worlds beneath our feet that felt equally alien and already existed. We just had to dig into the ground and spend time with them,’ the artist reflects. Spending time with foragers led her to think about the landscapes people carry in their minds, and how these can disappear alongside physical environments. A place, a species or even a familiar way of seeing the world can vanish from lived experience.

Her subsequent research into soil-dwelling animals informed projects such as meys, in which humans merge with social insects to become collective organisms. She is fascinated by species that survive in extreme conditions and may have developed forms of knowledge that humans have yet to understand. ‘There are many species that exist in extreme contexts and may have learned something about life that we don’t know,’ she says. The question of what humans might learn from other forms of life has become increasingly important to her work.

This curiosity informs Humeau’s collaborative process. Her projects bring together scientists, zoologists, anthropologists, historians and specialists whose knowledge exists outside established academic frameworks, including clairvoyants and geomancers. She is interested in what happens when different interpretations of the same place or phenomenon meet. Scientific expertise can explain the formation of a dust devil, for example, while a geomancer might describe it as a spirit or an energy moving through the landscape. ‘When you look at exactly the same landscape or site, you get all these different stories that somehow connect,’ she observes.

For Orisons, her monumental work in Colorado, Humeau worked with the farmers who owned the land, alongside soil scientists, botanists, ornithologists, conservationists, geomancers and clairvoyants. The project transformed an unfarmable piece of land, previously a potato field into an artwork, bringing her speculative worlds into contact with a living ecosystem. It followed an earlier site-specific project in Italy, made for Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo in 2021, which explored the origins of the vine flower in the context of a vineyard.

More recently, The Garden of Resuscitation in Norway has extended this interest in landscapes shaped by human activity. Set in a spruce forest once used for timber extraction, the project follows a piece of paper on a journey back to the forest from which its material originated, where it becomes a new, resuscitated tree. Humeau describes it as a monumental sculpture, a landscape and a garden, but also as the setting for a recurring ritual involving an elixir consumed each year. These works have led her to consider how artificial ecosystems might return to living environments and begin to evolve on their own. She is increasingly interested in artworks that can be activated, transformed and altered beyond her control.

For Humeau, looking beyond the human also means questioning the limits through which people understand intelligence, community and time. ‘We understand the world through our own bodies, our own lifespans, our own ideas of what intelligence is, and our own ways of connecting to others and forming communities,’ she argues. Yet life has developed countless other ways of existing. Considering these alternatives opens up questions about how humans might live differently and what they could learn from species whose survival strategies are far removed from their own.

The scale of geological and evolutionary time offers another way to unsettle human-centered thinking. ‘When you look at the history of humankind on the timeline of life, we’re just a tiny dot. We’re such a small fraction of time,’ Marguerite Humeau tells us. She recalls reading Orbital by Samantha Harvey, a novel about scientists aboard the International Space Station, whose repeated journeys around Earth shift between intimate personal experiences and the planet seen from a distance. One of the characters loses her mother while orbiting the Earth, holding personal grief against the vastness of the world below. Humeau is drawn to this movement between scales, from the immediacy of human life to the perspective of a distant observer.

Her interest in other forms of intelligence also extends to plants. During the pandemic, she began foraging in London with the help of a forager, paying attention to plants commonly dismissed as weeds. Their ability to grow in damaged, polluted or extreme environments can reveal something about the conditions of the ground they inhabit. Learning to recognize where they thrive becomes a way of reading a landscape and establishing a relationship with its other inhabitants. ‘Maybe they’re not communicating specifically with humans, but they’re still delivering a message, whether we choose to read it or not,’ she suggests. Imagination helps make these connections possible. The artist remembers spending one or two months in the Colorado desert while installing Orisons and making a film.

Although she felt alone in the landscape, she also experienced an intense sense of belonging to it. The stars above and the tunnels and burrows beneath the ground suggested a vast network of life, much of it invisible. ‘I felt I was part of a web of life that was mostly invisible but also very tangible. I could feel that I was part of it, even though I couldn’t see all of it,’ the artist recalls. That sensation, she suggests, may be close to the beginning of spirituality: the feeling of being connected to something whose nature remains unknown. Myths and stories emerge from the same impulse, giving shape to experiences that resist description. ‘We invent stories to make sense of that gap, of something we feel but cannot fully describe,’ she adds.

This continuing search for connection is now taking Humeau toward the future of human thought. She is researching dreams, regrets, anxieties and fears as territories that may still hold something beyond technological access, questioning what remains of private inner life as more of human experience becomes available to technology. The direction of this research is still open. Her work continues to ask what other worlds might exist alongside our own and what forms of imagination, ritual and attention might allow us to encounter them.

#9067. Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated

BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the New York and Paris-based designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.

“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

“Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”

“I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”

“You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen.

Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.

“When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he said. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”

“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”

At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

“Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he said. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”

“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.

“[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”

It was really a big experiment. In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky

Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.

“It was really a big experiment,” he said. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.

“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”

Much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.

“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he said.

“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.

But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project

“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”

His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

“It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he said. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”

“I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”

The competition to create something new and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.

“[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he said. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”

“I’m trying to find new materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.

“It’s like music – every year there is new songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”

After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.

“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he said. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”

“You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”

He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.

My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere

“I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in big development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev says these projects can be the most creative.

“The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he said. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”

“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”

Nuriev believes his most important role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was launched with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.

“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he said.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”

His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.

“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”

“As Coco Chanel said, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”

#9065. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#9063. how ifi lighting awakens human senses through precise illumination

treating light as an invisible building material, ifi lighting does not simply illuminate architecture, it illuminates the senses, giving physical form to atmospheres felt as much as seen.

mariana rodrigues November 20, 2026 3 min

Athens-based practice IFI Lighting shapes the way spaces feel, move, and linger in memory, treating light as an invisible building block of architecture. Guided by the ethos of Illuminating Senses, the studio cuts through the clutter of excessive lighting to accentuate tactile surfaces, frame crisp spatial lines, and direct movement with subtle restraint. Their approach bridges technical engineering with atmospheric sensitivity, delivering understated spaces that visitors feel as much as they see.

Founded in Athens in 1989 as Greece’s first dedicated architectural lighting studio, IFI Lighting established itself on the conviction that light belongs inside the structural concept from the very first sketch, shaping space alongside foundations and walls. Over three decades later, that vision drives an international practice bridging optical engineering, architecture, and sensory intuition. Led today by creative director George Anagnostakis and managing director Nickolas Anagnostakis, the multidisciplinary team designs across varied scales, from hospitality retreats to public landmarks, working directly with architects to sharpen and realize spatial concepts.

Approaching each commission as a collaborative co-author from the earliest structural sketches, IFI Lighting studies site topography, orientation, and tactile materials to anchor conceptual atmosphere directly into physical reality. Surface interaction studies and real-scale testing reveal how illumination catches diverse textures, allowing precise technical calculations to pair with atmospheric experimentation. Measured modulations between deep shadow and soft luminescence let a single volume reveal shifting moods throughout the day, while fixtures dissolve entirely into structural details to leave only the pure interaction between light and space.

Restraint also anchors the studio’s understanding of sustainability, transforming environmental responsibility into an architectural virtue that respects natural cycles. Prioritizing natural daylight, low-energy optical systems, and glare control helps the team curb light pollution at the source. Darkness ceases to be an empty absence, becoming an active medium that rests the eye, sculpts volumetric depth, and carves out pockets of calm intimacy within busy environments.

Rooted in ecological awareness and engineering rigor, the Athenian practice continually redefines contemporary architectural illumination. Grounding every installation in human perception, IFI Lighting proves that light conceived as a core structural material can reshape how we perceive, feel, and inhabit space.

#9062. SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

It is part of a wider renovation SOM announced for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.

#9061. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024
